title: OIDC Back-Channel Logout
subtitle: The IdP tells every app a user is signed out of by POSTing a signed logout_token server-to-server — the core step never touches the browser.

steps.label: User (or an admin) triggers logout
steps.lede: Something ends the SSO session — the user clicks “Log out” or an admin revokes the session at the IdP. This is where the chain starts.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools (F12) → Network tab, enable Preserve log so the redirect chain survives navigation. The important step of this flow will not appear here — that is the lesson.

steps.label: Logout reaches the end_session_endpoint
steps.lede: The logout is delivered to the IdP — typically via RP-Initiated Logout hitting end_session. The IdP clears its own session cookie and redirects back.

headers: idp_session=; Path=/; Max-Age=0; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=None

steps.devtools: Filter on end_session. Decode the id_token_hint (jwt.io / Auth Inspector) to read sub and sid — the session the IdP is about to tear down. Confirm the idp_session cookie is cleared with Max-Age=0.

steps.label: Terminate session, mint one logout_token per RP
steps.lede: The IdP terminates SSO session sid=abc123session, enumerates every RP that joined it, and mints a distinct logout_token (a JWT) for each — audience-scoped to that RP.
steps.code:
for rp in session.participants:            # RP1, RP2, …
  logout_token = sign(
    iss    = "https://idp.example.com",
    aud    = rp.client_id,                 # scoped to ONE rp
    events = { "http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout": {} },
    sub    = "248289761001",
    sid    = "abc123session",
    jti    = unique(), iat = now, exp = now + 120 )
  POST rp.backchannel_logout_uri  logout_token=<jwt>
steps.devtools: Not a network event you can see — it happens inside the IdP. Note the events claim is what distinguishes a logout token from a replayed ID token.

steps.label: POST logout_token to the RP (back-channel)
steps.lede: The IdP POSTs the logout_token directly to the RP’s backchannel_logout_uri. This request is server-to-server: it never traverses the browser, so it is invisible in the Network tab.

jwt.title: Decoded logout_token
payload: Issuer — must equal the expected OP
Audience — must contain this RP’s client_id
Unique id — cache it to reject replays
REQUIRED — marks this a back-channel logout
Session id — which specific session to kill

steps.devtools: You will NOT find this in DevTools. It is delivered IdP → RP over the back channel; capture it in RP access logs or a proxy (mitmproxy) in front of the RP. A common gotcha: a nonce claim must be absent — its presence means an ID token was replayed as a logout token → reject with 400.

steps.label: Validate the token, destroy the session
steps.lede: The RP validates the logout_token like an ID token — with two twists — then finds the session by sid and destroys it, revoking any refresh tokens. Handlers must be idempotent.
steps.devtools: Server-side: verify the signature against the IdP JWK kid=idp-key-2026 (alg not none), check iss, aud, iat/exp, that events is present and nonce is not, and that jti is unseen. Delivery is at-least-once — a repeated jti or an unknown sid must return 200, not error.

steps.label: Next visit finds no session
steps.lede: This is the only browser-side evidence the logout landed. On the next request the orphaned RP cookie matches no session, so the RP clears it and bounces the browser to re-authenticate.

headers: rp1_session=; Path=/; Max-Age=0; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax

steps.devtools: Filter on authorize. The Set-Cookie clearing rp1_session plus the fresh /authorize redirect is your proof the back-channel POST actually destroyed the server-side session.

steps.label: Signed out everywhere
steps.lede: Every RP that joined the session has been notified out-of-band. The user is signed out across all of them and must re-authenticate to continue.
steps.devtools: The value of the back channel: logout is reliable and driven by the IdP even if the browser is closed — but you must capture on the server to see it work. Contrast with front-channel logout, which is fully browser-visible but best-effort.
